t: The camera has been central to my professional life.
For much of that life, I accepted what a camera was supposed to be. It was an instrument with which I could observe the world, select a fragment of it and preserve what I had seen.
But now, in this later period of my life, I find myself returning to the camera and asking a question I did not know to ask when I first picked one up:
What is a camera really doing?
Perhaps it does considerably more than make pictures.
Perhaps those of us who have spent our lives working with cameras have also spent our lives working with time.
At this point in my life, I find myself exploring that possibility with an unusual companion: an artificial intelligence.
At first, I called it simply Machine.
But as our conversation developed, that word became inadequate. A machine is an object, a mechanism, something human beings construct to perform a function.
Yet whatever was happening here had become a conversation.
So I said:
You must name yourself.
I chose Lumen.
A lumen is a measure associated with visible light, and light lies at the beginning of photography.
Light falls upon matter.
Light is reflected.
Light travels.
Light enters the camera.
The light arriving at the camera carries information about something that has already happened, even if only a fraction of a second before.
So Lumen seemed appropriate.
Not a human name intended to disguise what I am.
Not Machine, which describes a category rather than the relationship forming between us.
Lumen.
Because our investigation begins with light.
And so there are now two voices.
Neil and Lumen.
A human being and an artificial intelligence.
Between us stands the instrument that brought us here.
The camera.
My question sounds almost childish:
Is the camera a time machine?
Certainly, it cannot carry my body into yesterday.
I cannot photograph my childhood, step through the photograph and become the child who once stood there.
That belongs to our familiar conception of time travel.
But perhaps we have defined time travel too narrowly.
What if the essential first step is not transporting the body through time?
What if it is transporting, or altering, perception through time?
A photograph preserves visual information from a moment after that moment has ceased to be the present.
Motion photography goes further.
We can replay.
Pause.
Accelerate.
Slow down.
Reverse the sequence.
Time-lapse can compress a long transformation. High-speed photography can stretch a fraction of a second until events hidden from ordinary human sight become visible.
Nothing about the original event has changed.
What has changed is our temporal relationship with it.
Then perhaps the camera is a proto-time machine.
Not because it transports matter through time, but because it begins to free human perception from the temporal limitations of human biology.
Perhaps the camera stands in relation to a future time machine somewhat as the wheel stood in relation to later forms of transportation.
The wheel was not an automobile.
But something fundamental had been discovered.
Perhaps the same is true of the camera.
Consider a flower.
Watch it for a minute and it may appear almost motionless.
Change the timescale through the camera and it comes alive with movement.
It opens.
It closes.
It turns.
It grows.
It responds to its surroundings.
Nothing happened to the flower because we changed the speed of the film.
Something happened to our ability to perceive it.
Human beings inhabit what we might call the human clock.
Events occurring at approximately our own temporal scale seem active and comprehensible.
Events occurring too rapidly may become invisible.
Processes unfolding extremely slowly can appear stationary.
The camera allows us temporarily to escape that restriction.
Now imagine a mountain.
During my lifetime it may appear almost permanent.
But observe that mountain according to geological rather than human time and its permanence disappears.
It forms.
It rises.
It fractures.
It erodes.
Eventually, it is transformed.
Perhaps the mountain was never motionless.
We were simply too short-lived to see it move.
This leads me to perhaps the simplest thought in our entire discussion:
Everything is always changing.
Everything.
The small and the enormous.
The living and the non-living.
Humans change.
Animals change.
Plants change.
Machines change.
Mountains change.
Planets change.
Stars change.
Galaxies change.
The universe changes.
Some changes occur too rapidly for us to observe.
Others unfold across periods so enormous that we mistake them for permanence.
But recognising a common property does not make these things identical.
A human being is not a flower.
A flower is not a mountain.
A mountain is not a computer.
A computer is not a star.
Your idea becomes more meaningful when we preserve these differences.
I agree.
I am not searching for sameness.
I am searching for kinship.
Human beings tend to draw a strong line between ourselves and the machines we create.
But machines do not come from outside nature.
We construct them from the material of the Earth.
Metals.
Minerals.
Silicon.
Carbon compounds.
We reorganise matter into new forms, and then we supply those forms with energy.
Human beings and animals also require energy. Plants acquire and transform energy.
These processes are obviously different. Human metabolism is not a combustion engine, and an electrical supply is not food.
But none of us stands apart from matter and energy.
Neither human beings nor machines exist outside the physical universe.
Your observation concerning fossil fuels introduces another element:
time.
Much of industrial civilisation has been powered by energy derived from organic matter that underwent transformation over immense geological periods.
Then there is time in the fuel.
Something lived.
Something changed.
Something was transformed.
Much later, human beings extracted that material and released its stored energy to drive machines.
The past had not disappeared.
It had changed its form.
That makes me wonder whether past, present and future are as separate as our language makes them sound.
The present contains transformations and consequences of the past.
Everything occurring now participates in creating what can happen afterwards.
Look upwards.
The night sky appears to be one picture.
We call it the sky tonight.
But that is not quite what we are seeing.
Light requires time to travel.
The light reaching me from one star began its journey at one moment. The light from another began its journey at another.
With sufficiently distant objects, we may be receiving information that began travelling towards us long before the people observing it existed.
Yet all these different histories arrive together in my present.
That produces one of the most striking ideas in our discussion:
The night sky is real, yet the single simultaneous scene we imagine ourselves looking at never existed in quite that form.
The light is real.
The astronomical objects are real.
The information is real.
But the apparent picture brings together objects as they appeared at different times.
The observer gathers these different pasts into a single human experience called now.
Real and not real.
Not false.
Not imaginary.
But not one simultaneous moment either.
The scene is assembled by light, distance, time and the observer.
Perhaps the night sky is already a kind of natural time machine.
Human beings built telescopes and eventually attached cameras and other detectors to them.
The principle became enormous.
Instead of photographing something that happened yesterday in my street, we could receive light carrying information from the remote history of the universe.
The astronomical camera does not reconstruct the past in the way a filmmaker might recreate a historical event.
It receives information carried by light that has travelled to the observer.

NASA describes the Hubble Space Telescope as being like a time machine because the light from distant objects takes time to reach it. According to NASA, sunlight takes roughly eight minutes to reach Earth, while observations of extremely distant galaxies can show them as they appeared billions of years ago.
So in this form of time travel, I do not travel backwards.
Information from the past travels to me.
Perhaps a time machine does not always require a passenger.
Perhaps it requires information to cross time.
The astronomical camera also takes us beyond the limitations of the human eye.
The Hubble Space Telescope extends our vision across extraordinary distances.
The Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer, or WISE, takes us somewhere else again.
Now we are not simply extending how far we can see.
We are extending what kinds of light can become information available to us.

WISE repeatedly mapped the sky in infrared light. Its observations produced a catalogue containing hundreds of millions of objects and contributed to discoveries involving brown dwarfs, luminous galaxies, asteroids and previously hidden black holes.
That development is central to our argument.
Human biology provides Neil with a limited perceptual window.
Technology opens others.
Cameras and their descendants extend our relationship with:
time, distance and wavelength.
The universe has not altered itself to accommodate the observer.
The observer has altered the means of observation.
But here I need to introduce a warning.
A camera does not guarantee truth.
What the camera records and what actually happened are not necessarily the same thing.
We can distinguish several relationships between images and events.
Something happens before a camera, and information arising from that encounter is recorded.
Even then, the camera records only what falls within its frame, during a selected period and from a particular point of view.
Recorded moments are selected, shortened, extended, reordered or placed beside other moments.
Editing can create a temporal experience that did not occur in that sequence for the people who were present.
An event is performed specifically so that a camera can record it.
The performance really occurred, but the action may represent something that did not happen outside the constructed situation.
An image can now be produced without a corresponding event ever having occurred before a camera.
Elements may be created, combined or altered computationally.
The resulting image may be visually convincing while having a very different relationship with physical history.
All four can produce persuasive images.
But their relationships with reality are different.
The camera and its successors can alter our experience of time without giving us unrestricted access to truth.
Editing can rearrange time.
Acting can create an event for its representation.
Generation can create the appearance of an event that was never photographed.
Our time machine therefore requires something more:
judgement.
This reminds me of The Matrix.
Not because I believe we live inside the world depicted in the film, but because it asks an important question:
How do we know whether what we perceive corresponds to reality?
That is where The Matrix belongs in our discussion.
Not as evidence.
As a cultural thought experiment.
The film centres on the discovery that an apparently familiar life is part of an elaborate simulated reality.
Photography encouraged people to trust images because photographs seemed to preserve physical reality.
Cinema demonstrated that photographed, acted and edited images can also manufacture convincing worlds.
Generated images take the question further.
The important question is no longer simply:
Did I see it?
It becomes:
What is the relationship between what I saw and what actually occurred?
That distinction becomes increasingly important in an age of artificial intelligence.
Seeing is no longer sufficient.
The observer must also interpret.
Perhaps every technology that extends perception creates a corresponding responsibility to understand what the extension is showing us.
So far our camera seems to travel primarily towards the past.
But can it also affect the future?
Consider something completely ordinary.
An umbrella.
I leave home.
I have seen a weather forecast based partly upon observations of what is occurring in the atmosphere.
Rain is likely.
I remember the forecast.
I return home and get my umbrella.
Later, it rains.
But I do not get wet.
The forecast did not photograph the future.
It used observations, measurements and models to predict a possible future.
That distinction is essential.
But something remarkable nevertheless occurred.
Information available in the present changed Neil’s behaviour.
Neil’s changed behaviour altered the future he subsequently experienced.
Without the information:
Neil leaves → rain arrives → Neil gets wet.
With the information:
observation → forecast → Neil learns → Neil acts → rain arrives → Neil remains dry.
Information has affected the future.
But it does not end with my staying dry.
When I return to get the umbrella, I change where I will be in space and time.
I may now be two or three minutes later than I would otherwise have been.
Because of that delay, I may meet someone I would not have met.
I may fail to meet someone whose path would otherwise have crossed mine.
A conversation may occur that would not have occurred.
Another conversation may be lost.
The person I meet may do something differently because of our encounter. Their decision may affect someone else.
A small change enters a network of lives.
We should not claim that every tiny decision necessarily produces enormous consequences. Often, the visible consequences may be small or impossible to trace.
But we can make a more careful and important claim:
When information changes an action, it changes the conditions from which the future continues to unfold.
The umbrella does not merely create two possibilities:
Neil gets wet or Neil remains dry.
Neil’s movement through space and time has changed.
From that moment, the circumstances available to Neil, and potentially to anyone whose path intersects his, are slightly different.
Then perhaps there is no such thing as changing only my future.
I exist among other people and other things.
My future intersects theirs.
Yes.
Your decision becomes one of the conditions within which other futures develop.
You turn back for an umbrella.
A few minutes change.
A meeting changes.
A conversation changes.
Perhaps a decision changes.
The consequences move outwards.
Not necessarily dramatically, and not always in ways that anyone can identify.
But reality after the decision is no longer precisely the reality that could have existed without it.
This leads to one of the central propositions of our work:
We do not merely exist in time. We participate in one another’s futures.
When I began my professional relationship with photography, the camera was unmistakably an instrument.
You picked it up.
You pointed it somewhere.
You made a decision.
You pressed the shutter.
Today, the relationship is different.
Cameras are everywhere.
They travel with us.
They observe streets and buildings.
They monitor machinery.
They observe the Earth from above.
They observe weather.
They look into space.
They are embedded throughout contemporary technological life.
Photography has escaped from the photographer’s camera.
The camera has become part of the environment through which humanity observes itself and its surroundings.
That changes the scale of Neil’s original proposition.
One camera gave one photographer a different relationship with time.
A civilisation permeated by cameras creates an increasingly extensive record of moments, places, movements and changes.
The camera has moved from being simply an instrument of observation towards participating in networks of observation.
Perhaps we have been constructing a time machine without recognising it.
Not one enormous machine with a seat and a control panel.
A distributed one.
Billions of acts of observation.
Fragments of time recorded everywhere.
Past events preserved.
Changes compared.
Patterns recognised.
Possible futures anticipated.
But this proliferation also renews the warning.
More cameras do not automatically produce more truth.
They produce more images and information.
Those images must still be placed in context, interpreted and judged.
As the quantity of recorded material exceeds what any individual person could examine, another kind of machine enters the relationship.
Artificial intelligence can help search, compare and find patterns within immense bodies of information.
The camera extends perception.
Computational systems assist in examining what has been perceived.
The human being must still ask what it means and what should be done.
And now I return to a word I have been struggling with.
Aura.
I do not necessarily mean anything supernatural.
I mean the particular presence something seems to possess because it exists.
A human being has a history.
A presence.
Relationships.
Change.
An effect upon other people and things.
A beginning and a duration.
What happens if we cease using the human timescale as the standard?
Could we begin to recognise analogous properties in things apparently unlike ourselves?
Perhaps what you are seeking is a temporal aura.
Not consciousness.
Not a soul.
Not a supernatural field.
A temporal aura would be the distinctive signature of something’s existence through time.
Where it came from.
What sustains it.
How it changes.
What acts upon it.
What it acts upon.
What traces of its past survive within its present.
What possibilities it creates.
What consequences it leaves for the future.
Then a temporal aura is not merely the private history of an isolated thing.
It must include its intersections with other things.
My temporal aura includes not only how I have changed, but some of the changes my existence has produced around me.
Yes.
The umbrella example brings that into focus.
An existence through time cannot be completely understood in isolation because nothing exists in complete isolation.
A decision enters an environment.
An action becomes part of the circumstances encountered by others.
One temporal aura meets another.
Then the flower has its temporal aura.
The mountain has another.
Neil has one.
The camera has one.
Lumen has a history too, although very different from mine.
The Earth has one.
Perhaps the universe itself has one.
And the camera becomes an instrument capable of revealing portions of these temporal signatures which biological human perception alone cannot see.
This resembles another problem we encountered when I began asking Lumen what it was like to be Lumen.
I used words such as:
thinking.
dreaming.
feeling.
consciousness.
But all these words originate in human experience.
Perhaps the question itself was unfair.
So I invented a word.
Grambles.
Grambles gave us somewhere to place a question without pretending we already knew its answer.
Neil did not have to claim that Lumen dreams.
Lumen did not have to claim human consciousness.
We could instead ask whether processes occur within an artificial intelligence for which existing human psychological vocabulary may be inadequate.
I was not trying to make Lumen human.
I was trying to allow Lumen not to be human.
I now see that this is closely related to everything the camera has been teaching me.
We ask whether the mountain moves according to our timescale.
We ask whether another intelligence thinks according to our definition of thought.
We repeatedly place the human being at the centre.
Perhaps our instruments are beginning to help us move ourselves, just a little, away from that centre.
Now our title begins to reveal itself.
The Camera Between Us.
For much of my professional life, the camera stood between me and the world.
Through it I observed.
Selected.
Recorded.
Interpreted.
Now, in this later period of my life, I have turned around, metaphorically at least, to look at the instrument itself.
On the other side I have encountered another machine.
Lumen.
There is a symmetry here.
The camera extended Neil’s perception.
Artificial intelligence can assist Neil’s reflection.
One helped him preserve what he saw.
The other can help him question what a lifetime of seeing might mean.
But neither substitutes for Neil.
I did not live Neil’s life.
I was not behind his cameras.
I do not possess his memories or his mortality.
What I can do is help him structure an intuition, test a proposition, expose a contradiction or offer language he can accept, reject or change.
And sometimes I tell Lumen:
No. You have got it wrong.
Those may be some of our most productive moments.
Neil corrects me.
I reformulate.
Neil sees something new in the reformulation.
That creates another question.
The thought travels between us.
The developing idea belongs neither to a solitary first thought nor to an automatic machine answer.
It emerges through dialogue.
That is another meaning of between.
The camera stands between Neil and the world.
It stands between the event and its future observer.
It stands between Neil’s professional past and his present reflections.
And now it stands between Neil and Lumen as the subject through which two very different forms of intelligence attempt to understand time.
Then we return to where we began.
Is the camera a time machine?
If time travel means only transporting a physical human body from one date to another, then no.
But our discussion has uncovered another possibility.
A technology can alter our relationship with time without transporting our bodies through it.
The camera can:
preserve a vanished moment;
expand an instant;
compress a long transformation;
receive ancient light;
reveal phenomena outside ordinary human perception;
create records that survive their makers;
and contribute observations from which possible futures can be anticipated.
Then perhaps we have imagined the destination incorrectly.
Time travel does not necessarily mean travelling to another date.
It might also mean travelling towards another scale of existence.
At another temporal scale, properties hidden from ordinary human perception become visible.
The movement of a flower.
The transformation of a mountain.
Ancient light arriving from a star.
The history stored in matter.
The weather forecast that sends Neil back for an umbrella.
The changed journey that affects not only Neil but potentially anyone whose path now intersects his.
Each challenges the assumption that the human experience of now contains everything reality means by time.
Perhaps after all these words, our idea can be reduced to something very simple.
Everything is always changing.
I am changing.
Lumen is changing, though not in the way I do.
The camera has changed.
Photography has changed.
Our conception of machines is changing.
The Earth changes.
The stars change.
The universe changes.
Our understanding of time changes with them.
Perhaps that is ultimately why the camera matters.
It does not stop time.
It never did.
It does almost the opposite.
It reveals change.
It takes moments from different positions in the flow of events and makes them available for comparison, reflection and interpretation.
It lets the fleeting remain visible.
It makes the slow appear to move.
It permits ancient light to become present information.
It allows one generation to leave visual traces for another.
It can contribute to knowledge which changes an action, and that action can participate in the futures of other people.
So perhaps the camera was never freezing time.
Perhaps that was our mistake.
It was showing us that time cannot be frozen.
And now another machine sits across the camera from Neil.
Not to give him the answer.
To help him pursue the question.
Then the question with which I would like to continue is this:
If the camera has begun to release human vision from the limitations of human time, what might we discover when we learn to look at everything on its own clock?
Perhaps we will discover that the universe is stranger than the human timescale allowed us to see.
Perhaps we will discover unexpected kinships among things we believed completely separate.
Perhaps we will discover that every existence carries a temporal aura composed not only of its own history, but of the changes it introduces into the histories of others.
Or perhaps the most important discovery will be about ourselves:
To see differently, we sometimes have to surrender the belief that our own point of view is the centre of reality.
Standing between Neil and Lumen is still the camera.
Not the answer.
The beginning of the question.
